title: Network Reconnaissance Triage
summary: Read a simulated Nmap service scan of a lab file server and decide what deserves attention first.
objective: Interpret scan output, separate open from closed ports, and turn findings into a defensible recommendation.
scenario: You are the junior analyst on a lab hardening project. A teammate ran an authorised service scan against hr-file-01, a file server in the isolated 10.10.24.0/24 lab network, and pasted the output below. Nothing was exploited and no live system is involved. Your job is triage: what is exposed, what is risky, and what do you tell the system owner?

evidence.title: nmap -sV -Pn 10.10.24.15
evidence.content:
# nmap -sV -Pn 10.10.24.15   (LAB TARGET - simulated output, no live scan)
Starting Nmap 7.94 ( https://nmap.org )
Nmap scan report for hr-file-01.lab.local (10.10.24.15)
Host is up (0.00042s latency).
Not shown: 994 filtered tcp ports

PORT     STATE  SERVICE       VERSION
21/tcp   closed ftp
22/tcp   open   ssh           OpenSSH 7.2p2 Ubuntu 4ubuntu2.8
23/tcp   open   telnet        Linux telnetd
80/tcp   open   http          Apache httpd 2.4.29 ((Ubuntu))
139/tcp  closed netbios-ssn
445/tcp  open   microsoft-ds  Samba smbd 4.7.6-Ubuntu (workgroup: LAB)
3306/tcp open   mysql         MySQL 5.7.33-0ubuntu0.16.04.1
8080/tcp closed http-proxy

Service Info: OS: Linux; CPE: cpe:/o:linux:linux_kernel
Nmap done: 1 IP address (1 host up) scanned in 12.44 seconds

evidence.title: Asset context
evidence.content: hr-file-01 stores HR documents and is reachable from the general staff VLAN. There is no jump host in front of it. The server owner believes only file sharing is exposed.

questions.prompt: Which ports are reported OPEN in this scan?
questions.hint: Read the STATE column, not just the port numbers.
questions.explanation: Five ports are open: 22, 23, 80, 445 and 3306. Ports 21, 139 and 8080 are reported closed, which means the host answered but nothing is listening. Filtered, closed and open are three different states and mixing them up leads to false findings in a report.

questions.prompt: Which open service should receive attention first?

options.label: 22/tcp OpenSSH 7.2p2, because SSH is a remote access service
23/tcp Telnet, because the protocol has no transport encryption
80/tcp Apache 2.4.29, because web servers are always the biggest risk
445/tcp Samba, because file sharing is the server's job

questions.explanation: Telnet is the standout. It transmits usernames, passwords and session data in cleartext, and a modern network has no reason to run it when SSH already exists on the same host. SSH, HTTP and SMB all need review, but none of them is broken by design the way Telnet is.

questions.prompt: Explain why that service is a problem and what you would do about it.
questions.placeholder: Example shape: the protocol does X, an attacker on the network can therefore do Y, so we should do Z.

concepts.label: Credentials or session data can be captured
Disable it and use SSH instead

questions.model_answer: Telnet carries credentials and commands in cleartext, so anyone able to sniff traffic on the staff VLAN can capture the login and replay or reuse it. Disable telnetd and use the SSH service already running on port 22.
questions.explanation: A complete answer names the protocol weakness (no encryption), the attacker capability it creates (credential capture on a shared network), and a concrete fix (disable telnetd, standardise on SSH). Naming only one of the three is a partial answer.

questions.prompt: MySQL on 3306 is reachable from the staff VLAN. What is the best recommendation?

options.label: Change the MySQL root password and leave the port open
Bind MySQL to localhost or restrict 3306 to the application hosts that need it
Move MySQL to a non-standard port so scanners miss it
Nothing, the database is protected by its own authentication

questions.explanation: Reduce exposure first. A database should listen on localhost or be filtered to specific application hosts. Password rotation is good hygiene but does not remove reachability, and port shuffling is security by obscurity that a -p- scan defeats in seconds.

questions.prompt: The scan also shows Apache 2.4.29 and OpenSSH 7.2p2. What is your next investigative step for those versions?
questions.placeholder: Describe what you would look up and what you would do with the result.

concepts.label: Check the versions against known vulnerabilities
Patch or upgrade the outdated packages

questions.model_answer: Look up CVEs published against Apache 2.4.29 and OpenSSH 7.2p2, confirm the build is really unpatched rather than a backported distro package, then schedule a patch or upgrade with the server owner.
questions.explanation: Version banners are a starting point, not a finding. Correlate the version against a vulnerability source, confirm the distro has not backported fixes, then drive it to a patch decision.

concept: Reconnaissance output is data, not conclusions. Value comes from mapping each open service to the exposure it creates for that specific asset, then ranking by what an attacker on that network could realistically do.
remediation: Disable Telnet and standardise on SSH with key based authentication
Bind MySQL to localhost or filter 3306 to named application hosts
Patch Apache and OpenSSH, then rescan to confirm the change
Document the intended service baseline so future scans are diffs, not surprises
